Since the early 2000s, neurotechnology research has provided ample evidence that it is possible to directly interface with the brain, learn details of function or dysfunction from brain recordings, and use the results therapeutically.
Thus, neurotechnologies could improve the lives of many patients in ways that are currently impossible using more traditional approaches such as pharmaceuticals.
Comprehensive biological insights and technical breakthroughs have been made possible by introducing increasingly capable and specific methods to interact with the brain.
Given the promise of neurotechnologies to improve people’s lives, it is not surprising that we have seen an explosion of technical demonstrations.

These technologies combine neuroscientific protocols, hardware, software, signal processing and artificial intelligence (AI) to derive meaningful information about brain function or to replace, restore, improve, enhance or supplement lost functions caused by different neurological disorders1.
Not surprisingly, these demonstrations have caught the interest of scientists, engineers, clinicians, funding agencies, the venture capital community and the public.
Moreover, neurotechnologies are now routinely the subject of high-profile articles and even covered in popular media.
Despite these demonstrations being encouraging and inspiring, so far only a few new products provide life-changing (and otherwise unavailable) therapeutic benefits (Fig.

In brain–computer interfacing (BCI), one area of neurotechnology, issues with translation have been recognized for over 20 years; they were the central theme of the Second International BCI Meeting, which was held in 2002 and was aptly named ‘Brain–Computer Interfaces for Communication and Control: Moving Beyond Demonstrations’.

Although this recognition has led to discussions (and often heated debates) about the shortcomings of different technologies and their improvements, systematic discussions about the requirements of and recommendations for generating neurotechnology solutions that are actually used in patients have been scarce2,3.
In this Review, we identify and highlight the problems facing neurotechnologies by providing guiding principles and recommendations to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of these devices.

Here, we focus specifically on adaptive interactions with the human brain in which stimulation is contingent on the state of the brain (that is, closed-loop), because their complexity (and consequent need for analysis) is substantially higher than for more conventional peripheral nerve stimulation that is provided continually (that is, open-loop)4.
Neurotechnology components Any adaptive neurotechnological solution takes advantage of existing neuroscientific knowledge to address an important problem.

For this purpose, it uses technology that consists of several components: hardware that interacts with the brain; software that acquires signals from the hardware and delivers feedback to the user or caregiver through an output device (such as a computer screen or electrical stimulator); and signal processing/AI algorithms that extract relevant features from brain signal recordings (or other physiological or behavioural signals) and translate them into informative outputs.
Hardware Several hardware technologies exist that support interactions (mostly electrical) with the brain at different scales.

Owing to fundamental laws of biophysics, interactions at the smallest scales (which here we call microcircuits, functional systems and interregional circuits) generally require invasive implantation, whereas interactions at the largest scales (which here we call macroscale aggregates) can be achieved using non-invasive methods (Table 1).
Microcircuits Cortical microcircuits exist in different structures on the scale of less than a millimetre.

Most relevant to our discussion are cortical columns — vertically organized structures in the human neocortex that are approximately 100 µm wide and that include excitatory pyramidal cells and inhibitory interneurons.

They can be understood as individual units of information processing such that, for example, different columns provide distinct sensory receptive fields in the somatosensory5 and visual6 systems, and are related to different directions of movement in the motor system7.
Several probes have been designed to support extracellular recordings and stimulation of individual neurons within cortical columns (that is, microelectrode recording; Fig.
2 top left), although most of them are optimized for basic neuroscience studies in animals (such as the Michigan probe or Neuropixels8) rather than for clinical use in humans.
The most widely known probe is the Utah array9 that has been extensively used in both humans and animals.

Interaction with microcircuits in the brain using these types of probes produces data (action potential firing rates and local field potentials) from individual and small groups of neurons that are invaluable for basic research on such microcircuits.
However, the complexity of system configuration and operation, as well as limited long-term recording stability10, seriously limit translation.
Functional systems Many cortical columns together form functional systems of the order of a few centimetres that are often organized topologically and accessible on the lateral surface of the cortex.

For example, in the visual, somatosensory, motor and auditory systems, neuronal populations respond to different regions of the visual field, sensation, motor movements or different frequencies of perceived sounds (retinotopy, somatotopy, mototopy and tonotopy, respectively).
The most common way to interact with functional systems is through subdurally placed electrodes.
Called electrocorticography (ECoG), this technique has been clinically used in humans for decades, primarily for presurgical mapping of function and epileptic foci in patients with epilepsy11 (Fig.
Owing to its accurate and direct interaction with the human brain, ECoG has provided important scientific and clinical insights.
Typical electrode configurations in humans are 1–3 mm exposed diameter and 3–10 mm spacing (total electrode count 64–256).

Thus, these electrodes cannot detect activity in individual or small groups of neurons, but rather provide access to different signal signatures produced by spatially separated neuronal populations representing different functions, such as individual fingers12 or the mouth13.
These signal signatures include traditional evoked potentials, the local motor potential14, and, most relevant in the present context, low-frequency oscillations and broadband gamma.

Low-frequency oscillations (such as those in the alpha (8–12 Hz) or beta (18–25 Hz) ranges) are rhythmic changes in ongoing cortical activity15,16 which are related to cortical excitability, that is, the probability of cortical excitation in response to inputs17,18,19.
By contrast, broadband gamma activity is widely recognized as a direct reflection of the population-level activity of neurons directly underneath the electrode20,21,22,23.
Thus, the detection of low-frequency oscillatory activity and broadband gamma provides direct physiological interpretations of neuronal populations across a particular functional system.
Furthermore, ECoG activity can provide useful information about pathological activity such as high-frequency oscillations24.

Stimulation of the brain through trains of stimuli applied to ECoG electrodes has been used for decades for functional mapping11, and new methods for single-pulse stimulation25,26 and high-frequency stimulation27 are refining the interrogation of brain structure and function.
Finally, because ECoG electrodes are much larger than their potential movement across the brain, they provide excellent short-term and long-term stability28,29,30.

ECoG’s stability and ability to record and modulate specific aspects of functional systems is useful not only for basic research but also for translational applications such as restoration of movements31,32, communication functions33, speech34,35, reducing the frequency of epileptic seizures36, and stroke rehabilitation37.

Interregional circuitry Different functional systems together form interregional circuits, such as the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loop that is affected by movement disorders such as Parkinson disease.
Interregional circuits put functional systems (such as those generating movements, sensations or emotions) in the context of overall behaviour.

Because several important structures of such interregional circuits (such as the subthalamic nucleus) are not located on the lateral convex surface of the cortex, but are instead deep inside the brain, the only way to interact with them directly is through recording/stimulation with electrodes that can reach these deep structures (deep brain stimulation (DBS) and stereoencephalography (SEEG); Fig.
Although the electrode configuration of these devices can access different areas in the brain, the electrode size is approximately on the same scale as those of surface ECoG electrodes.
Thus, DBS and SEEG electrodes capture signals similar to those detected by ECoG.

Interregional circuits are suitable targets for disorders that result from an imbalance in regulation of a specific function, as is the case in movement disorders38, Tourette syndrome39 or — according to early but encouraging evidence40 — mood disorders such as depression.
Macroscale aggregates Access to microcircuits, functional systems and interregional dynamics currently requires invasive methods.

However, non-invasive focused ultrasound stimulation41,42, temporal interference stimulation43,44 and functional ultrasound45 might, with some improvements in availability, accuracy and practicality, provide levels of brain access similar to invasive techniques.
At present, invasive methods provide the most direct and hence efficacious access to microcircuits, functional systems and interregional dynamics.
By contrast, non-invasive devices measure electrical or other physiological macroscale aggregates without penetrating the skull (such as electroencephalography (EEG)) (Fig.

Because non-invasive sensors are further away from neuronal population(s) and closer to fields generated by sources outside the brain, they detect not only the electrical fields generated by many millions of neurons (that is, a far-field effect) but also different types of artefacts.
Moreover, there are always several orders of magnitude more independent sources of electrical fields (neurons or synchronously active cortical columns) than sensors.

Thus, it is not only impossible to detect direct reflections of individual neuronal populations due to the far-field effect; it is also mathematically impossible to unmix/reconstruct such asynchronous population-level activity from the macroscale aggregate20.

The only electrical signals that have a direct physiological explanation and that can be detected non-invasively are low-frequency oscillations, which are putatively produced by coordinated series of action potential volleys by brain nuclei that simultaneously hyperpolarize large areas of the cortex46.
Despite these limitations, non-invasively detected brain signals have provided useful diagnostic information about brain function or have treated different neurological disorders47,48.
For example, EEG is routinely used in the clinic to monitor people’s sleep49 or to diagnose epilepsy50.
In addition, EEG can detect different aspects of depression or anxiety51,52,53,54,55, reveal signs of mild traumatic brain injury56, or measure cognitive function related to dementia57.

EEG can also be used to establish a new brain-based communication or control option in people with severe paralysis58,59,60,61,62,63,64,65,66,67,68,69, or to restore motor or speech function lost after stroke70,71,72,73,74 or cervical spinal cord injury75.

Moreover, open-loop non-invasive brain stimulation protocols (such as using repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, or transcranial direct or alternating current stimulation) can improve symptoms of various disorders including major depression76, obsessive compulsive disorder77 or schizophrenia78.
However, treatment effects often diminish over time79, probably because the chronic activity imbalance underlying these disorders cannot be permanently modified using such open-loop protocols80.
This may also partly explain the discrepancy in efficacy described in recent reports using 40-Hz open-loop visual stimulation81,82.
Closed-loop neuromodulation protocols83, in which stimulation is contingent on the state of the brain or of behaviour, are more effective and lead to long-term plasticity84,85,86.
These closed-loop protocols have even been conducted using auditory stimulation where they improved slow-wave sleep87,88,89,90 or provided access to human emotions91.
Non-invasive approaches offer several advantages and disadvantages.
They are affordable, and they can be easily applied without surgery and removed after device operation92,93.

Nonetheless, they are also intrusive, obtrusive, or less robust when used during daily life activities, and they cannot readily sense or stimulate specific (and in particular deep) structures in the brain, thereby putting distinct and probably unavoidable limits on precision and efficacy.

Fortunately, recent device innovations have improved the practicality and robustness, for instance detecting EEG in or around the ear or on the forehead so that the sensors can be applied rapidly and minimize challenges introduced by hair.

Software, signal processing and artificial intelligence From the 1950s to the 1970s, that is, in the early days of neurotechnology development, most components of the systems were realized by hardware94.
By contrast, any modern neurotechnology system consists mainly of software.

Several robust and free toolboxes (for example, BCI200095,96 or OpenViBE97) or commercial software programs (such as Simulink) now aid the design and dissemination of modular and portable real-time neurotechnology systems98, including an early version of a general-purpose invasive neuromodulation platform for human use99.
Although these software systems have reduced the time and cost of neurotechnology development, they still require a team of highly skilled experts for their operation.

Ideally, development kits should be produced that can make useful EEG-based measurements (such as sleep stages) readily available to software engineers without specialized training in hardware development, physiology or AI.
Neurotechnology software interacts with sensor/stimulation hardware to interface with the brain.

It also implements signal processing/AI algorithms that can identify and decode relevant information from brain signals, calibrate decoding algorithms to a user’s brain signal characteristics, and filter artefacts from undesirable sources such as muscles, the recording setup or the environment.
Decoding algorithms extract the different brain signals relevant to invasive and non-invasive signals100,101,102,103,104,105 and translate them into outputs for diagnosis or treatment.

Although increasing practicality of decoding algorithms is important and has received some attention, there have been persistent arguments for the need for more complex feature extraction or translation algorithms106 to improve performance, despite only little evidence of substantial improvements, in particular at the same level of tuning by an expert.
Meanwhile, current feature extraction algorithms are not well matched to the characteristics of the brain signals they are trying to extract107,108.

For example, the fast Fourier transform, a technique to extract a signal’s frequency spectrum based on the assumption that individual frequency components are sinusoidal in shape, is commonly used to extract brain activity related to low-frequency oscillations although it is widely known that those oscillations are not sinusoidal109.
Thus, improved integration of knowledge about brain signal characteristics can improve performance109,110.

Because non-invasive sensors detect signals from many (time-varying) sources in the brain, decoding algorithms must be calibrated to each user, often before each session and sometimes even during use.
This calibration process consists of data collection from the user and configuration of the decoding algorithm by an expert based on the results.
Generally, improving the decoding algorithm’s performance requires increasing the sensor count, the manual tuning and/or the amount of calibration data111,112, which greatly reduces practicality.
AI advances (such as deep learning) and their integration into closed-loop neurotechnologies could minimize the need for initial or ongoing calibrations.
A deep learning model can be trained on a large number of subjects and be applied with little or no additional calibration in individual users112,113.

However, collecting the requisite large dataset still faces practical and ethical challenges, especially because it might need to be trained using data from healthy people as well as different patient populations.
Artefacts can greatly reduce the robustness of a neurotechnology system, in particular for non-invasive systems.

These artefacts can be detected114,115 and removed from brain signals to a certain extent116,117,118,119, but the methods usually only work for data from a specific task or type of artefact (such as eye movements), or require additional reference data that have to be collected.
Thus, there is currently no widely accepted automated and general method to determine to what extent signals are clean and not contaminated by artefacts, or to remove artefacts from brain signals.
One fundamental limitation is that there is no detailed empirical or mathematical definition of brain or artefactual signals.

Thus, despite notable advancements (such as active electrodes), the current main strategy to deal with artefacts is to minimize them by using the neurotechnology system in carefully controlled environments and with users who are instructed to minimize movements.

In summary, the two biggest shortcomings of current signal processing/AI algorithms are the need for lengthy and/or recurring calibration by experts, and their applicability to limited number of settings, environments or behaviours.
Requirements for translation Despite the described shortcomings, there is now substantial knowledge of brain functions and the associated protocols that can modify them.
Moreover, readily available, capable and affordable sensing and stimulation hardware, software and signal processing/AI algorithms now exist.
However, to turn these components into solutions that can impact the health or other aspects of quality of life for many people, several requirements need to be considered.
Incremental benefit Perhaps the most important requirement is that the neurotechnology needs to provide sufficient incremental benefit — that is, benefit over existing solutions.

In this context, suggesting benefit by documenting ‘statistical significance’ is suboptimal; statistical significance indicates confidence that a particular neurotechnology has some non-random diagnostic or treatment effect (for example, of improved symptoms).
A finding of statistical significance is the typical requirement for publication in scientific or engineering journals.

In marked contrast, clinical studies require findings of ‘clinical significance’, which refers to the smallest diagnostic or treatment effect that provides a meaningful benefit to the target population.

Thus, a successful neurotechnology solution needs to provide at least a clinically significant improvement in efficacy (or other benefit such as reduced cost, increased efficiency or reduced morbidity) over the standard of care.
Because they indicate large effect sizes, clinically significant improvements will usually also be statistically significant.
Acceptable cost or risk The cost of the neurotechnology should not exceed its benefit.
Despite the regulatory challenges and a complex ecosystem of medical devices120, new technologies are adopted once the benefit to a person exceeds the cost to the person121.
In this context, the risk associated with the neurotechnology (for example, due to implantation) is a component of its cost.
Practicality The neurotechnology needs to be practical, that is, it needs to be beneficial despite the constraints in capability and resources in its intended usage environment.

Thus, if intended to be used at home, it needs to function without undue preparations and with no or minimal assistance by others (such as clinicians, engineering experts, caregivers or family members).

When considering the practicality of a component or neurotechnology solution, it is useful to compare it with a relevant established technology (for example, responsive neural stimulation versus vagus nerve stimulation, or EEG-based brain monitoring versus smartwatch-based body monitoring).
Reliability The neurotechnology needs to be reliable, that is, it needs to work for a large fraction of its intended target population most of the time and in most environments.

This requirement is explicit for invasive neurotechnologies, which are subject to strict standards for reliability (for example, basic electrical standards such as EN 60601-1-2), biocompatibility and biostability (such as EN 10993-x), mechanical stability (such as ISO 14708-1), radiofrequency immunity and human factors (such as EN 62366), as well as emerging standards for adaptive systems (such as EN 60601-1-10).

Non-invasive neurotechnologies are not subject to the same level of reliability standards (presumably because device failure often does not cause immediate harm to the user), but reliability is still implicitly required as it will otherwise greatly hamper adoption.
Supportive ecosystem To be widely adopted, any solution needs to be supported by an ecosystem that assists, manages and rewards the interactions with all the involved parties.
For example, specific mental health conditions such as depression are currently supported by such a system.

Clinicians know how to diagnose depression with several established and clinically validated questionnaires or other tools, interpret their results, prescribe antidepressants, follow the results of the treatment and request reimbursement for their services.
Moreover, the pharmaceutical industry has established sales and marketing channels, as well as training opportunities.

By contrast, although DBS has some aspects of such an ecosystem (such as established reimbursement and at least somewhat standardized procedures), perhaps owing to its reduced practicality (such as the requirement for a skilled neurosurgeon) and increased cost compared with drug-based therapy, DBS is still more of an isolated solution that is offered and understood by only selected providers and medical centres.
No meaningful ecosystem currently exists for most other neurotechnologies.

Regulatory approval Most neurotechnologies are subject to regulatory approvals according to different classifications that are related to patient risk: class I devices (such as tongue depressors) require little regulation, class II devices (such as transcranial magnetic stimulators or non-invasive rehabilitation systems) require more explicit design controls, and class III devices (such as DBS and other chronically implanted recording or stimulation devices) warrant substantial design controls, verification tests and other quality control measures.
In addition, the design process for medical devices requires a quality management system where the internal audits and controls are also stringent.

Regulatory approval can present serious challenges to translation, in particular for class II and III devices, as safety and efficacy must be addressed even for pilot work in a small number of patients.

In this section, we briefly highlight these challenges in the United States, contrast them to those in other countries such as Australia, the European Union (EU) and China, and draw conclusions in the context of neurotechnology development.

Regulatory approval requires establishing user needs, assessing risk and mitigating issues with detailed plans, reviewing the design through its development with independent parties, verifying that the neurotechnology meets the design requirements, validating clinical efficacy and demonstration of meeting user needs through trials, and finally proving that risks are managed to an acceptable level.

Furthermore, it involves detailed tests for biocompatibility and the design of the stimulation protocol, an assessment of MRI risks, and human factors for eventual errors from the patient, caregiver or clinician.
In the United States, the regulatory processes mandated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have advantages and disadvantages compared with those in other countries.

For example, the FDA provides guidance to innovators throughout the lifecycle of their project by supporting the design control process and piloting clinical studies through the pre-submission process and the Early Feasibility Program.

Moreover, the FDA initiated the ‘breakthrough’ designation that provides additional regulatory support and guidance for new technologies that might represent a larger step of innovation, with more risks but higher benefits if the technology is ultimately successful.
Synchron’s Stentrode, which integrates electrodes into stent technology to access the nervous system through the vascular system, has taken advantage of the breakthrough pathway.
Finally, the FDA is seeking to allow parallel submission for regulatory and reimbursement applications.
With these procedural innovations, the FDA aims to address the perception of increased regulatory hurdles and quality management requirements that might stifle innovation.
Innovators in the United States also have access to less traditional routes of approval, but with other constraints.

For example, orphan neurotechnologies that target rare disorders can apply for a humanitarian device exemption (HDE), which requires demonstration that the claimed benefits might save substantial clinical trial costs.

However, the HDE includes certain limitations (such as a prohibition on profit) to ensure that the process is not abused by companies trying to circumvent the more traditional and stringent approval pathways.
The humanitarian pathway still requires safety assessments, design controls and risk mitigations as expected for class III devices, among others.
These limitations might explain why few companies are pursuing this route of approval for new neurotechnologies.
Regulatory agencies in other regions have different risk/benefits for neurotechnology innovators.

For example, Australia is an attractive environment because exploratory studies can be approved by local ethics committees instead of the Therapeutic Goods Administration, Australia’s regulatory agency.

This is ideal for proof-of-concept studies, which probably aided the first-in-human studies (Synchron’s Stentrode, the Neurovista epilepsy seizure forecasting system, and the Epiminder epilepsy seizure recorder) that started in Australia.

The EU is currently in the process of implementing an updated set of regulatory requirements, the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), which added new regulatory requirements for new innovations and even requires substantial updates to existing device dossiers.
In addition, the EU relies on ‘notified bodies’, which are private companies that act as an intermediary between governmental regulators and technology companies.
The MDR is greatly reducing the number of notified bodies, which will increase approval time and thus risks stifling innovation in the EU.

The Chinese FDA, instead, offers simplified procedures, but it often requires prior approval in a company’s home market, which limits the innovation pathway to incumbent Chinese companies or at least requires the creation of a strategic partnership.

In summary, the complexity of regulatory requirements seems to be increasing across the globe, but some countries (such as the United States and Australia) are providing mechanisms for innovators to receive early confirmation of device performance.
However, the EU is facing great hurdles as the MDR is implemented, and the absence of an equivalent to the Early Feasibility or Breakthrough designation further exacerbates the situation.
Commercial viability Knowing how to create a new neurotechnology solution does not automatically incentivize people to build it, maintain it and make sure that it improves people’s lives.

Indeed, research funding and the research sponsored by it sometimes benefits research subjects, and there are also government programmes that provide incentives for clinically useful medical technologies that can help people with rare diseases (such as FDA’s HDE programme).
However, for a neurotechnology solution to improve people’s lives on a large scale and over the long term, it needs to be commercially viable.

For example, the FreeHand122, ActiGait123 and Second Sight’s Argus retinal implant124 are neurotechnologies that undeniably provided considerable benefits to their users, but the absence of commercial viability forced their organizations to stop providing and supporting them, with negative consequences for early adopters125,126,127 (Box 1).
Commercial development begins with the initial investment to satisfy regulatory demands.
These costs are substantial, in particular for class III devices with new components or mechanisms of action.

For example, current estimates to develop a new class III medical device, from concept to premarket approval (PMA), are US$94 million, with US$75m (80%) spent on the testing and validation (such as packaging, transport, cleaning, sterilization, mechanical stability, electrical safety, biological/toxicological/histopathological safety and compatibility), fulfilment of standards (for example, ISO 9002) and applications necessary for regulatory approval128.
This is a considerable barrier for any technology development project attacking a mature market, and of even greater concern for invasive neurotechnologies that attack new and unproven markets.

Thus, development of an appropriate regulatory strategy, and concomitant adjustment of technology development and financing approaches, needs to be an integral component for any class II or III device from the beginning.

It is essential to define a deployment strategy early in the project; investors generally like to see a well-defined risk burndown that helps focus on addressing fundamental issues as early as possible in the design process.

Examples might include using an established device to confirm a new therapeutic mechanism of action (for example, brain stimulation for improving memory using a device that was approved for Parkinson disease) before investing in a device optimized to the new disease to demonstrate some level of target engagement with existing technology.
Similarly, Synchron’s Stentrode leveraged an existing technology for intravascular stent placement to accelerate development of its sensing technology.
A staged approach with clear milestones can help to manage the investment risk and ensure all constraints are considered in a minimally viable product prototype.
In the long term, a solution can only be commercially viable if its benefit exceeds its cost and if there is a market that is large enough to provide sufficient incentives.

A medical solution’s benefit is usually measured in quality-adjusted life years (QALY), that is, the improvement in quality of life (measured from 0–1) of a person times the number of years with such improvements.
Because most neurotechnologies are currently not meant to save lives, their opportunity to confer benefits is mainly to improve a person’s quality of life.
Clinical protocols should be designed to ensure that this information is gathered early to assess the perceived value of the new method.

Any new solution should not have total costs (the solution’s price plus any additional costs such as diagnostics, surgery, physician management, and patient risks, for example from surgery) exceeding the QALY value assignment, which is approximately U$50–100k per QALY in Western health economics129 (Fig.
Regarding market size, it is important to consider the investment required to bring new solutions to the market.

Based on estimates from previous investments into neurotechnology companies (such as Neuropace, Nyxoah or Neurolutions), we estimate go-to-market costs to be of the order of US$10m over 4 years for a non-invasive solution and US$100m over 10 years for an invasive product.

Investors will demand a reasonable risk-adjusted rate of return; therefore, to account for development risks and the time needed to ramp up sales, for an attractive investment case, the market potential needs to be substantially (of the order of 10 times) higher than the investment.

Assuming the simplified investment costs listed here, and exemplary selling prices of US$2,000 and US$20,000 per unit (for non-invasive and invasive solutions, respectively), a commercially viable solution would require a market of 50,000 patients per year who need the benefits offered by the device, are good treatment candidates and would choose to use it (US$100m/$20k = 50k, or US$10m/$2k = 50k for invasive and non-invasive solutions, respectively).

Although we acknowledge that all neurotechnology investment cases are likely to deviate from these assumptions (in cost, time and possible returns), the investment decision processes will follow similar principles.
The relationship between benefits and other factors substantially influences adoption of neurotechnologies.
A case in point is DBS implants for movement disorders, which are widely recognized as effective, and are approved and reimbursed in many countries.

Although detailed numbers are difficult to determine, 30 years after the introduction of DBS130, only less than 3% of patients with Parkinson disease receive a DBS implant131, although this number seems to be a sizable fraction of all eligible patients132.
Nonetheless, compared with drug treatment/best medical therapy (BMT), DBS is certainly not mainstream clinical practice (Fig.
This picture seems to be roughly comparable to that seen for cochlear implants (depending on the definition of eligibility, 2.1% or 12.7% adoption amongst eligible patients133).

Although the causes for limited adoption of DBS are likely to be complex (including important nuances about differential efficacy over time or reduced practicality for DBS versus medication-based treatment), a review of the literature revealed that DBS restores approximately 0.1 QALY per year more (loosely speaking, a 10% increase in quality of life) than the alternative best medical treatment such as Levodopa134 (Fig.
Even though the heterogeneity of patient groups make the results difficult to compare, cochlear implants and hearing aids seem to fare similarly in this sense.

Both technologies can be used to restore hearing in people with moderate hearing loss, and research found that cochlear implants restore approximately 0.07 QALY per year more than hearing aids135,136,137.

In conclusion, it is encouraging that DBS, as an electrical intervention, provides a clear benefit over conventional pharmaceuticals, but it is also worth noting that other factors (such as high cost, risk and impracticality of DBS) cause many patients or their doctors to decide against chronic DBS implantation.

Life-sustaining technologies such as the cardiac pacemaker have overcome this adoption chasm to reach the vast majority of patients by further improving efficacy (for example, using rate-adaptive pacing) or practicality (endovascular placement without a thoracic surgeon and conditional safety for MRI).
DBS is likely to require similar improvements in efficacy, practicality and other factors to increase its rate of adoption.
In any case, the adoption time and rate of DBS can provide a meaningful yardstick for the development of other invasive neurotechnologies.
Challenges for translation In this section, we identify and summarize general challenges that have received little attention so far.

Novelty and complexity Building neurotechnologies and ensuring their successful long-term adoption requires the development of new technology components; their integration into a neurotechnology system that realizes a neuroscientific protocol designed to address the user need; validation of the system in the context of its designated clinical or mass-market population; design of a supporting ecosystem complementing the many other existing (and often more validated, simpler and cheaper) approaches; education of end-users, clinical personnel and other stakeholders; building and maintaining a team of experts; and acquiring the funding to support it.

Addressing these requirements involves deep neuroscientific, technical, clinical, regulatory and business expertise, as well as substantial funding, time, and full appreciation of the unique opportunities and limitations of neurotechnologies.

Additionally, there are two distinct challenges that need to be overcome: first, both traditional academic research laboratories and corporate settings are not optimally positioned to pursue these efforts, because even the largest academic research groups often do not have all the required expertise in-house.
Moreover, academics get rewarded (by research papers or grants) for advances in knowledge in their specific narrow field.
Thus, they are usually (and necessarily) less interested in understanding and integrating components across domains.
By contrast, although corporate settings can acquire expertise across domains, recruiting high-level expertise from academia is expensive and may be impractical.

Moreover, companies are often required to deliver a return on investment with reasonable certainty and in a short or at least predictable amount of time, which is almost impossible given the issues described above.

The second main challenge is to identify senior leadership who, beyond the daunting task of securing funding, can assemble a team of experts and direct them to a path with reasonable chance of clinical and commercial translation despite the existing challenges.
Finding leadership with the requisite comprehensive and multidisciplinary expertise is exceedingly difficult.
The ‘Anna Karenina’ principle The famous opening line of Leo Tolstoy’s ‘Anna Karenina’138 was adapted and popularized by Jared Diamond139 into what is now known as the ‘Anna Karenina’ principle.
It states that success of any endeavour depends on many factors, whereby a deficiency in any of these would cause the whole effort to fail.

Translated to neurotechnologies, although the individual components do not need to be perfect, best-of-class or even state-of-the-art, any neurotechnology solution can only be successful if all requirements for translation are addressed to a satisfying level.

Thus, if the technology does not provide enough incremental benefit, is too costly, impractical or unreliable, is not supported by a comprehensive ecosystem, does not have all necessary approvals or is not commercially viable, the outcome is always the same: it cannot address the problem it promises to solve, regardless of how exciting it may seem to domain experts or the general public.

The inconvenient (but necessary) question raised here is then whether a translational neurotechnology research direction should be pursued or sponsored even when it is evident that it cannot satisfy all the above-mentioned requirements even with foreseeable improvements.
Given the reality of funding constraints, it seems reasonable for funding agencies, investors and scientists to pursue research directions with realistic chances of leading to viable solutions.
Importantly, these statements apply to translational research only and are by no means intended for basic research.
No silver bullet Similar to software engineering140, there is likely to be no singular technical advance (‘silver bullet’) in neurotechnology that would guarantee the emergence of new solutions.

Although it is desirable to steadily improve technologies, and despite many solutions remaining out of reach without such improvements, several published opinions suggest that success of a neurotechnology crucially depends on a specific technical feature (such as the ability to record from individual neurons141,142,143,144 or the sophistication of a particular signal processing approach106), or that enough improvements in an individual technical component (such as more electrodes or a more powerful wireless transmission chip) will aid or even result in valuable new neurotechnology solutions (the fallacy of the magical component).

Instead, the Anna Karenina principle suggests that new solutions can emerge only when all neurotechnology components (hardware, software and signal processing/AI) are aligned with a suitable neuroscientific protocol such that together they can address all requirements for translation.
Focus on individual components Overemphasizing the optimization of the performance of an individual component might be not only of little help, but even detrimental to practical solutions.

For example, the design of chronically implantable sensors or adaptive neuromodulation systems using (clinically unproven) state-of-the-art electronics or manufacturing techniques can impede or preclude regulatory approval.

Likewise, optimizing one feature of a neurotechnology component (for example, maximizing channel count, like in recent invasive and non-invasive technology innovations, or increasing the complexity of the decoding/calibration algorithm) might lead to detrimental effects on another trait (for example, increasing reliance on signal processing experts, or increasing duration of setup or calibration).
Outlook In this section, we provide recommendations for how to avoid, or at least mitigate, the challenges mentioned in previous sections.

Addressing these points should enable scientists, engineers, clinicians and companies to prioritize or optimize their research and development plans, and thereby accelerate the translation of neurotechnologies that can realistically and over the long term improve people’s lives.
Assess and validate potential benefits The central requirement of any new technology is to provide sufficient benefits over existing solutions.

The assessment of such benefits can be performed by evaluating their use in the target population and target environment, using metrics of health economics (such as QALY) or a relevant form of effect size (for example, the Action Research Arm Test145), and by contrasting the results to those of existing (and often simpler, cheaper or more practical) solutions (for example, implanted neurotechnologies versus pharmaceuticals; closed-loop versus open-loop DBS stimulation; brain-based versus muscle-based communication; brain-based versus behavioural diagnoses).

Advance and integrate scientific knowledge By definition, the motivation of any neurotechnology is based on neuroscientific knowledge, which is often only partially integrated into the device function.
For example, current approaches to minimize the frequency of epileptic seizures are based on the knowledge that electrical stimulation can disrupt the formation of seizures.

However, no systematic protocol with information about the specific resting-state or task-related connectivity in a specific patient exists that could be used to optimize the detection or treatment of seizures.
Developing such user-specific protocols would be likely to improve device efficacy.

Many translational neurotechnology studies report on the potential benefit for a particular problem, but only few of them are designed to inform about the principles governing the use of the neurotechnology (such as the relationship between specific neuromodulation protocols with plasticity85).
Thus, advances in basic neurotechnology research would improve our understanding of not only the technical components, but also their interaction with the underlying neurological substrate.
The limitations of current brain sensing technologies have greatly restricted our ability to understand brain functions.
For example, the thalamocortical circuits for movement and the disorders associated with them are often treated with DBS.

The anatomical connections between key areas of the motor system (such as the subthalamic nucleus, thalamus or motor cortex) are more or less known, as well as that stimulation of some of these areas reduces tremors associated with Parkinson disease or essential tremor.
Nonetheless, the specific mechanism for each of these processes is unknown, as are the reasons for variation in efficacy146,147.

For other neurological or psychiatric disorders (such as chronic pain or depression), knowledge of the underlying neural system is much less developed and often cannot be readily acquired because there are no relevant animal models for these disorders.
Thus, human neuromodulation studies tend to be based on poorly grounded hypotheses and are essentially forced to be expensive multi-year trial-and-error experiments.

Such limitations have led to variability in results (for example, in DBS used to treat depression148) or have contributed to the failure of clinical trials (such as the Everest trial (NCT00170716)) and their companies (such as Northstar Neuroscience149).

Because invasive human research is complex and expensive, only a few such studies have been conducted, which greatly limits the opportunities to acquire new knowledge that can lead to more educated hypotheses.
This conundrum could be referred to as the chicken-and-egg problem of invasive neurotechnologies.
One potential solution is to acquire a more complete understanding of task-related brain activity and connectivity, and of the neural or behavioural effects of stimulation of different targets.

In the absence of even more suitable technologies, SEEG in patients with epilepsy150 and advanced methods to evaluate these recordings in response to certain tasks151,152 or electrical stimulation25 could enable large-scale studies to be conducted and provide at least some information.
To the best of our knowledge, such comprehensive studies are not yet underway.

Optimizing technology innovation Development of neurotechnology solutions begins with technical and scientific development, proceeds to clinical development (such as using an investigational device exemption), then to commercial/regulatory development and finally to development and application.
This process is complex, time consuming, risky and expensive.

Thus, creating new solutions is currently only practical and commercially viable for the largest problems, barring tremendous capital allocation with low or unrealistic expectations of return on investment (ROI).
To mitigate this issue, general-purpose technology platforms can be developed to improve practicality or cost of technology and scientific development (Fig.

For invasive systems, a general-purpose and modular hardware/software platform can be envisaged that can support different types of (ideally standardized) sensors/stimulators, has sufficient computational capabilities, has connectivity to external monitoring/computational units, and comes with proven closed-loop protocols (such as beta-triggered stimulation), proper documentation and regulatory support (for example, in the United States, a Rights of Reference letter to access the master file established with the FDA).

A master file contains all relevant technical documents and supporting validation tests prepared by the manufacturer, and a Rights of Reference letter provides a potential applicant of an investigational device exemption with the right to access and reference that information.
Examples of established invasive platforms are Neuropace’s Responsive Neurostimulation System36,153, Medtronic’s PC+S154, Medtronic’s Summit RC+S155,156 and Medtronic’s PERCEPT157.
Examples of emerging platforms or platform components are CorTec’s BrainInterchange99,158, Synchron’s Stentrode159, Precision Neuroscience’s platform and Neuralink’s Link160.

The established platforms enable clinicians, researchers and neuroengineers to explore new therapies for Tourette syndrome, depression and obesity, in addition to advancing existing therapies for movement disorders and epilepsy.

Since 2001, the Cleveland Functional Electrical Stimulation Center has been developing the Networked Neuroprosthetic System161, which uses functional electrical stimulation to restore upper-extremity function in people with chronic stroke.
The NIH HORNET programme is looking to open-source this system to make it available to the general community.
In the future, new systems with enhanced software capabilities will expand the utility and usefulness of such existing hardware platforms99.

For non-invasive systems, a practical and affordable closed-loop research platform can be envisioned that consists of hardware, software, signal processing/AI and neuroscientific protocols that together provide useful and clinically validated outputs (such as sleep stages, measurements of cognitive function, correlates of depression or biomarkers of seizures) or treatment functionality (for example, using auditory stimulation).
These platforms could take advantage of existing hardware (such as from Emotiv, g.tec, Neurable or Neurosity) and software (such as BCI200095), which would favour future solution developers.
Notably, general-purpose platforms and focused solutions have fundamentally contradictory goals.
The goal of platforms is to reuse the same technical components to reduce development time and cost, whereas focused solutions aim to optimize technical components to improve function.
Thus, although platforms are desirable, they do not reduce the need for focused solutions.
Well-designed platforms are particularly useful during early testing where many approaches are being evaluated to quickly de-risk a new therapy or technology.
Once the proof-of-concept is demonstrated, simplified and specialized solutions for the final user can be developed.

Focus on the user A key recommendation is that neurotechnology research and development needs to make the creation of solutions for important problems of humanity its central purpose rather than an ancillary one.

This suggestion not only challenges domain experts (such as electrical engineers) to learn more about completely unfamiliar domains (such as clinical neurology), but also prompts funding agencies and research organizations to reward solution-oriented interdisciplinary work.
It also challenges scientists, funding agencies and journal editors to appreciate the substantial difference between inspiring technical demonstrations and pragmatic but valuable solutions.

Focus on the ‘right’ problem Neurotechnologies that aim to have an impact on people’s health need to focus on those problems that can be addressed with existing technologies and scientific knowledge (or their foreseeable improvements).

This seemingly obvious suggestion has important implications; for example, with any current sensor technology, brain signals are noisy compared with signals detected from ocular or other muscle movements.

Thus, it is challenging to support solutions such as brain-based communication or control functions that confer substantial clinical benefits over existing muscle-based solutions in a large number of patients without an as-yet unidentified paradigm shift in sensor technology.
Instead, diagnostic applications of brain signals might more readily provide clinically relevant benefits.
For example, clinical diagnosis of sleep is routinely performed by evaluating 30-s segments of EEG data49.

Likewise, brain-based neuromodulation/neurorehabilitation solutions can provide beneficial plasticity; for instance, with appropriate electrical stimulation and conditional rewards, the spinal cord of animals162 and humans163 can be reliably conditioned over many trials to produce larger or smaller outputs even when the measurements of those outputs in each trial are very inaccurate.
Brain-based stroke rehabilitation71,72,74,164 supports the same conclusion.

Thus, given the current technological limitations, it appears to be prudent to focus on diagnostic and neuromodulation/neurorehabilitation applications, and to seek new and potentially disruptive concepts for interacting with the brain.

In conclusion, designing neurotechnologies that can widely affect people’s health requires selection, implementation and optimization of the main components (neuroscientific protocols, hardware, software, and signal processing or AI algorithms) to meet all the requirements discussed in this Review.

The chances of clinical and commercial translation can be increased by focusing on the needs of the user and on problems that can be solved realistically given known limitations; by increasing and implementing scientific knowledge; and by optimizing technological innovations by leveraging general-purpose platforms.

Abstract Advancements in decoding speech from brain activity have focused on decoding a single language.
Hence, the extent to which bilingual speech production relies on unique or shared cortical activity across languages has remained unclear.

Here, we leveraged electrocorticography, along with deep-learning and statistical natural-language models of English and Spanish, to record and decode activity from speech-motor cortex of a Spanish–English bilingual with vocal-tract and limb paralysis into sentences in either language.
This was achieved without requiring the participant to manually specify the target language.

Decoding models relied on shared vocal-tract articulatory representations across languages, which allowed us to build a syllable classifier that generalized across a shared set of English and Spanish syllables.
Transfer learning expedited training of the bilingual decoder by enabling neural data recorded in one language to improve decoding in the other language.

Overall, our findings suggest shared cortical articulatory representations that persist after paralysis and enable the decoding of multiple languages without the need to train separate language-specific decoders.
Similar content being viewed by others Main Anarthria—loss of the ability to articulate speech1—can be a severe symptom of neurological conditions such as stroke and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
Invasive speech brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) that decode cortical activity into intended speech are being developed to restore naturalistic communication to patients with anarthria and paralysis.

Specifically, intracortical electrodes, stereo-electroencephalography and electrocorticography (ECoG), the last of which directly records electrical signals from the cortical surface, can capture neural activity relevant to produced speech2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9.
However, speech-BCI advancements have largely focused on decoding a single language, primarily English or Dutch, owing to study-population sampling3,5,6,7,8,10,11,12,13,14,15.
A focus on monolingual and English decoding is not unique to speech neuroprosthetics; there are parallel trends in automatic speech recognition and language modelling.
Therefore, language technologies for bilingual speakers, as well as speakers of non-English languages, are often less developed16,17.
Approximately two-thirds of the world population are bilingual, that is, they proficiently speak two or more languages18.
Research indicates that the multiple languages an individual speaks serve complementary functions for communication.

For instance, bilinguals often report using their languages (L1-native and L2-acquired; in some cases, L2 may also be native) in distinct speaker and social contexts and further report that the languages they speak contribute distinct dimensions to their overall personality and worldview19,20,21,22.

To develop a neuroprosthesis capable of restoring embodied communication to all who could benefit, regardless of language background, it is essential to design BCI systems capable of multilingual decoding.

To naturally decode bilingual sentences, it is desirable for the system to flexibly infer the intended language of the participant entirely on the basis of cortical activity and/or natural-language models, which capture language-specific word-sequence statistics.

It is unclear whether intended language can be decoded directly from cortical activity in common speech-motor areas such as the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG, including Broca’s area) and the sensorimotor cortex (SMC).
A shared articulatory (vocal-tract motor) representation across languages would allow models to generalize rapidly, minimizing required training time and burden on the participant.
However, this would present a challenge in decoding the intended language from cortical activity alone.
The extent to which shared representations or language-specific activation patterns exist in speech-motor cortex is unclear.
Some evidence suggests that multilingualism may alter core speech-motor networks21,23,24.

Specifically, learning a non-native second language (L2) may recruit distinct patterns of cortical activity25,26,27,28 or evoke stronger activity in regions of the speech network such as the IFG or SMC29,30,31,32,33,34.
In support of shared representations between L1 and L2, recent work has shown that the same general anatomical regions tend to be activated across languages35,36,37,38.
In addition, the brain may fit a non-native L2 into the articulatory framework of L1, forming, for example, shared syllable representations and speech-motor patterns30,39,40.

Bilingual speech production has primarily been explored with functional magnetic resonance imaging, leaving an open question for how the precise temporal dynamics underlying shared or distinct cortical representations enable decoding.
Here we report the development of a bilingual speech neuroprosthesis for a Spanish–English participant with severe anarthria and paralysis (ClinicalTrials.gov; NCT03698149).

During attempted speech, we decoded neural activity from the speech-motor cortex, recorded with a 128-channel ECoG array, word-by-word into English and Spanish phrases, using a vocabulary of 178 unique words.

The intended language is primarily inferred by scoring candidate-decoded sentences with English and Spanish language models, incorporating the differential statistical patterns of word sequences in each language that build through a sentence.
Despite the participant learning English later in life, neural activity patterns, particularly those important for decoding, are shared, with no language-specific electrodes.
We demonstrate that these shared activity patterns best represent the articulatory content of speech and facilitate the generalization of a syllable classifier across languages.

Building on this result, we show that performance on a vocabulary in a given language can be improved and expedited by utilizing training data previously collected in the other language, thus reducing the required time and burden for bilingual participants to use all their languages.

Results Performance of the bilingual speech neuroprosthesis We designed a system capable of flexibly decoding English and Spanish phrases in a participant with paralysis and anarthria due to brainstem stroke (ClinicalTrials.gov; NCT03698149).
Our models were trained on neural features from a high-density, 128-channel ECoG array primarily covering the left sensorimotor cortex and inferior frontal gyrus.
During each phrase-decoding trial, the system displayed a single English or Spanish phrase on the screen as the current target.

The phrase-decoding system continuously recorded local field potentials (LFP) from each electrode in the ECoG array and extracted relevant neural features, specifically high-gamma activity (HGA; 70–150 Hz) and low-frequency signals (LFS; 0.3–100 Hz; Fig.
1a and Extended Data Fig.
The participant volitionally activated the system by attempting to speak, and this initial speech attempt was identified by a speech-detection module.
Once this initial attempt was detected, the phrase-decoding system activates and presents a series of ‘go’ cues every 3.5 s.
In each 3.5-s window, the participant attempted to say a single word.

The vocabulary, referred to as bilingual words, consisted of 51 English words, 50 Spanish words and 3 words shared between languages (no, a, and the participant’s nickname, Pancho; Supplementary Table 1) for a total of 104 words.
Within each cued window, the neural features were streamed to a classifier trained to emit probabilities over the bilingual words (Fig.
1a and Extended Data Fig.
These probabilities were then split for English and Spanish words.

Given that verbs and adjectives, especially in Spanish, may have multiple different conjugations, we broadcasted the predicted probability for the unconjugated form of the verb to all the conjugated forms.

For example, the predicted probability for the word ‘traer’ would be broadcasted to the words in the set {traer, traigo, traes, trae, traemos, traen, trayendo}, and the probability for the word ‘bring’ would be broadcasted to the words in the set {bring, brings, bringing}.
This led to an increased vocabulary size of 111 Spanish and 70 English words for a total of 178 unique words (67 English, 108 Spanish and 3 shared; Supplementary Table 2).
We then applied a beam search to combine probabilities with separate monolingual natural-language models trained in English or Spanish.
The use of natural-language models prioritizes linguistically valid phrases and properly conjugates verbs on the basis of preceding and following context.
A composite score was generated for phrases in each language that reflect a combination of neural predictions and phrase likelihood under the language model (LM).
As a final step, an integrator module chose the highest-scoring phrase across the two languages to display on the screen.
As speech attempts were being made by the participant, the speech-detection module continued to predict speech events.
The decoding system monitored these events over the course of the trial and deactivated when a speech attempt was not detected in the preceding 3.5-s window.
The system then advanced to the next trial after a brief delay.
Classification and detection models were trained before phrase decoding with an isolated-target task.
In this task, a single bilingual word was presented on the screen, and the participant attempted to produce the target word at a visual ‘go’ cue.
The HGA and LFS features spanning from the ‘go’ cue to 3.5 s after the ‘go’ cue were used to predict the target bilingual word.
We evaluated our decoding pipeline using a copy-typing task similar to our past work13.
The participant was prompted with randomly interleaved English and Spanish phrases, which he tried to replicate (Supplementary Videos 1 and 2).
During evaluation, decoding models were trained using data exclusively from preceding sessions with no ‘day-of’ recalibration.
To measure performance, we primarily used the word error rate (WER) metric, commonly used to evaluate outputs of automatic speech recognition systems and communication BCIs13,41,42,43.

One way this may manifest is in a shared syllable representation across languages30,39,40.

Rapid transfer learning between languages Transfer learning is a common technique in machine learning that involves the initialization of model weights with parameters learned on a separate task or dataset55,56.
Transfer learning has primarily been used in neural decoding to leverage models trained in previous participants to expedite training in a new participant57,58.
